Roussel, 'The Microarchitecture of the Pentium 4 Processor,' IEEE Micro, vol. 21, no. 2, pp. 20-30, March-April 2001 (page range less certain); same paper as the Intel Technology Journal, vol. 5, no. 1, Q1 2001 version you already own; nothing was published in 2007

sources.title: Closing the Gap Between ASIC & Custom: Tools and Techniques for High-Performance ASIC Design
sources.venue_or_publication: Kluwer Academic Publishers (book, D. Chinnery & K. Keutzer; later Springer reprint)
sources.what_it_covers: ASIC-side techniques for attacking the performance/design-closure gap versus full-custom: physical synthesis, floorplanning, wire planning, useful skew, buffering/gate sizing, methodology; organized around a running high-performance core case study.
sources.why_relevant: The closest thing to a book-length design-closure war story: it is written as 'here is where ASIC flows break (timing, area, wiring, power) and here is what teams actually do to recover,' so it maps directly onto congestion/timing-closure entries.
sources.verification_hint: search: Chinnery Keutzer "Closing the Gap Between ASIC & Custom" Kluwer 2002 ISBN 0-7923-7500-6

sources.title: The Pentium Chronicles: The People, Passion, and Politics Behind Intel's Landmark Chips
sources.venue_or_publication: Wiley-IEEE Computer Society Press (book, Robert P. Colwell)
sources.what_it_covers: First-person account of the P6 and Pentium 4 programs: the architectural and implementation gambles, schedule slips, design/validation crises, and how the teams dug out of them.
sources.why_relevant: One of very few nameable, public, first-person Intel accounts of a design going off the rails and being rescued; useful as a project-level failure/recovery source even where it is not PD-tool specific (covers the NetBurst frequency/power wall context).
sources.verification_hint: search: Colwell "The Pentium Chronicles" Wiley 2006 ISBN 978-0470050176

sources.title: The Implementation of POWER7: A Highly Parallel and Scalable Multi-Core High-End Server Processor
sources.venue_or_publication: IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits, vol. 46, no. 1 (D. Wendel, R. Kalla, et al.)
sources.what_it_covers: Circuit and physical implementation of POWER7 in 45nm: floorplan and partitioning, clock and power distribution, eDRAM integration, frequency/power bring-up results.
sources.why_relevant: Same genre as the Warnock POWER4 physical-design paper you own, but two generations later and at a new node — implementation papers in this series routinely document what failed on first silicon/closure and what was changed (grid, clock skew, thermal). Flagging it is in-family with your owned set.
sources.verification_hint: search: Wendel "The Implementation of POWER7" IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits 46(1) 2011

sources.title: Power Distribution System Design Methodology and Capacitor Selection for Modern CMOS Technology
sources.venue_or_publication: IEEE Transactions on Advanced Packaging, vol. 22, no. 3 (L. D. Smith, R. E. Anderson, D. W. Forehand, T. J. Pelc, T. Roy)
sources.what_it_covers: Chip/package/board power-delivery-network design: target impedance, decoupling capacitor selection and placement, simultaneous-switching noise, with measured hardware results.
sources.why_relevant: The citable classic for the power-grid leg of your registry — IR-drop / dI/dt failures and the decoupling/rework fixes, written by practitioners out of a real Sun design environment.
sources.verification_hint: search: Larry Smith "Power Distribution System Design Methodology and Capacitor Selection for Modern CMOS Technology" IEEE Transactions on Advanced Packaging 22(3) 1999

sources.title: ESNUG (the 'ESNUG' moderated chip-design mailing list), archived on DeepChip.com
sources.venue_or_publication: deepchip.com — moderated e-mail list founded/edited by John Cooley, running since 1992
sources.what_it_covers: Practitioner-submitted posts (often named engineers, often anonymized) about real projects: tapeout disasters, EDA tool surprises, congestion/timing blowups, ECO and re-spin recoveries, silicon bring-up surprises.
sources.why_relevant: The longest-running public, searchable archive where working physical-design engineers post actual failure-and-recovery episodes rather than sanitized methodology; a natural hunting ground for named war stories to add to the registry.
sources.verification_hint: search: ESNUG deepchip.com John Cooley ESNUG post archive; browse http://www.deepchip.com/items/ for numbered ESNUG issues

sources.title: SNUG (Synopsys Users Group) proceedings — user-authored physical-design / timing-closure case-study papers
sources.venue_or_publication: SNUG (Synopsys Users Group) conference proceedings, annual, multiple regional SNUG events and SNUG World
sources.what_it_covers: Practitioner papers on real tapeouts: congestion and timing-closure rescue flows, CTS experiments, ECO methodology, signoff escapes — written by the design teams that hit the problems.
sources.why_relevant: Highest-density venue for genuine ASIC closure war stories that are individually citable; caveat for your registry: the value is in specific papers, so individual titles must be harvested from the proceedings index rather than from this series name alone.
sources.verification_hint: search: SNUG Synopsys Users Group proceedings timing closure physical design case study paper (also index at solvnet/ Synopsys SNUG paper archive)

sources.title: EETOP forum (bbs.eetop.cn) digital-back-end / tapeout-failure discussion threads
sources.venue_or_publication: EETOP 集成电路论坛 (bbs.eetop.cn), '数字后端设计' / 'IC设计' boards
sources.what_it_covers: Chinese-language practitioner threads on 布局布线 congestion, 时序收敛, 流片失败/改版 (re-spin), and bring-up debugging, with teams narrating what broke and what they changed.
sources.why_relevant: Large public corpus of first-person PD failure-and-recovery narratives that English-language registries almost never index; individual threads need to be named before use.
sources.verification_hint: search: eetop 论坛 数字后端 时序收敛 流片失败 改版 经验
